title: India Approves First Polymer Banknote Trials for ₹10 and ₹20 Notes
excerpt: The government greenlights RBI field trials of one billion plastic notes each in two denominations, reviving a decade-old plan to make low-value currency more durable and harder to counterfeit.
body:
• The Union government has approved RBI field trials for polymer banknotes, starting with one billion pieces each of ₹10 and ₹20 denominations.
  • Polymer notes last 2.5 to 4 times longer than paper and incorporate advanced security features including transparent windows and micro-optic holograms.
  • The government explicitly denied viral claims that paper currency would be withdrawn, confirming existing notes remain legal tender.
  • Over 30 countries including Australia, the UK, and Canada already use polymer banknotes for some or all denominations.

India is set to join more than 30 countries that use polymer banknotes after the Union government approved the Reserve Bank of India's proposal to conduct field trials with plastic currency. Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary confirmed in Parliament that the RBI will introduce one billion pieces each of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes on a trial basis.

Why ₹10 and ₹20 First

Low-denomination paper notes cycle through millions of hands daily — from vegetable vendors and tea stalls to auto-rickshaws and small shops. They wear out fast. Paper notes in these denominations typically become unusable within 12 to 18 months, forcing the RBI to constantly print replacements at significant cost.

The ₹10 and ₹20 denominations make up roughly a quarter of all physical currency notes in circulation by volume but account for just 1.3% of the total value. That makes them ideal test candidates: high turnover, low financial disruption if the trial produces unexpected results.

The RBI's printing subsidiary, Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited, has already floated a global tender to procure 3.4 crore polymer sheets with integrated security features.

What Makes Polymer Different

Polymer banknotes are printed on thin, flexible sheets of biaxially oriented polypropylene film. Despite the "plastic" label, they are lightweight and foldable, handled much like paper notes. The key advantages are practical rather than cosmetic.

Durability is the headline benefit. Global studies cited by the RBI indicate polymer notes last 2.5 to 4 times longer than paper equivalents, surviving four to five years of heavy daily use. They resist dirt, moisture, and tearing more effectively because their non-porous surface does not absorb sweat, grease, or water — a meaningful advantage in India's tropical and monsoon climates.

Security is the second major draw. Polymer substrates allow central banks to embed features that are difficult to replicate on paper, including complex transparent windows, color-shifting metallic foils, and micro-engraved optical elements.

No, Paper Currency Is Not Being Withdrawn

The approval triggered a wave of misinformation on social media, with viral posts claiming the RBI planned to withdraw all paper currency and replace it with plastic notes by June 30, 2026. The Press Information Bureau flagged the claims as false and urged citizens to verify information through official sources.

"According to RBI, there are no plans to withdraw paper currency notes or replace them with plastic currency notes by June 30, 2026."

— PIB Fact Check

RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra confirmed that polymer notes remain at a preliminary stage and that existing paper currency will continue to circulate normally. The PIB also flagged a video using a digitally altered voice resembling Prime Minister Modi to falsely claim that paper notes would be discontinued.

A Decade in the Making

India's polymer currency experiment is not new. The RBI first proposed field trials for ₹10 polymer notes between 2009 and 2012, identifying five cities — Kochi, Mysuru, Shimla, Jaipur, and Bhubaneswar — for real-world testing. Technical challenges around procurement, material sourcing, and specialized printing delayed the rollout for over a decade.

The 2026 approval marks the first time the initiative has advanced to official government sanctioning alongside global supply tenders. Australia pioneered polymer currency in 1988 and completed a full transition by 1996. The United Kingdom, Canada, and Singapore followed in subsequent years.

What It Means for Everyday Cash

The field trial will evaluate how polymer notes perform across India's diverse climate zones, from extreme northern heat to coastal humidity, and under everyday handling practices including folding, crumpling, and pocket storage. If successful, the technology could save the RBI hundreds of crores in currency replacement costs annually while delivering cleaner, harder-to-counterfeit notes to the public.
nri_angle: NRIs who regularly handle rupee cash during visits home will encounter more durable, cleaner notes in lower denominations — and the polymer shift mirrors currency modernization already underway in the UK, Canada, and Australia.
